blocks.content: Public Interest Litigation is intended to bring justice within the reach of the poor, disadvantaged, and ignorant masses who are unable to approach the court for relief.

rows: Strictly restricted to the person whose legal rights are directly infringed.
Relaxed; any public-spirited individual or organization can approach the court.
Vindication of individual private rights and personal disputes.
Protection of public interest, constitutional rights, and social justice.
Strict adherence to formal procedures, pleadings, and court fees.
Flexible procedures; courts can act on informal letters or ex-officio cognizance.
Adjudicative and neutral referee between opposing parties.
Affirmative and inquisitorial, frequently issuing continuous directives and monitoring implementation.

items: PIL cannot be filed solely against private individuals; state or public authority involvement is mandatory.
Matters related to landlord-tenant disputes, service matters, and admissions to educational institutions are explicitly excluded from being entertained as PILs.
The Supreme Court and High Courts can treat simple letters or telegrams from citizens as PIL petitions (Epistolary Jurisdiction).

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) relaxes the traditional legal rule of 'Locus Standi' to enable access to justice for marginalized groups.
The concept of PIL originated in the United States in the mid-1960s as Social Action Litigation.
In India, PIL was introduced by the judiciary under the leadership of Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer and Justice P.N. Bhagwati.
A PIL can be filed in the Supreme Court under Article 32 and in any High Court under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution.
Matters concerning environmental pollution, bonded labor, custodial violence, and human rights violations are widely entertained under PIL.
